This vignette uses the R package **TSP** [@Hahsler+Hornik2007]. Please cite the package and the accompanying Journal of Statistical Software paper (see `citation("TSP")`) when you use it in your work.

Finding the shortest tour is NP-hard, so the number of tours that would have to
be checked for an exact solution grows factorially with the number of cities.
For this reason, **TSP** offers fast heuristics that find good (but not
necessarily optimal) tours and an interface to the exact solver Concorde. This
vignette describes the implemented methods and shows how to choose and compare
them. All methods are called through the same function:

```r
solve_TSP(x, method, control, ...)
```

where `x` is a `TSP`, `ATSP` or `ETSP` problem, `method` selects the algorithm,
and additional arguments (or the list `control`) set method-specific
parameters. The result is a `TOUR` object. See `?solve_TSP` for the complete
list of parameters.

## Overview of the methods

| Method argument | Algorithm | Type | Problems | Control parameters |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `"identity"`, `"random"` | Order in the data / random order | construction | TSP, ATSP | `rep`, `opt`, `verbose` |
| `"nn"` | Nearest neighbor | construction | TSP, ATSP | `start`, `rep`, `opt`, `verbose` |
| `"repetitive_nn"` | Nearest neighbor from every start city | construction | TSP, ATSP | `opt`, `verbose` |
| `"nearest_insertion"` | Nearest insertion | construction | TSP, ATSP | `start`, `rep`, `opt`, `verbose` |
| `"farthest_insertion"` | Farthest insertion | construction | TSP, ATSP | `start`, `rep`, `opt`, `verbose` |
| `"cheapest_insertion"` | Cheapest insertion | construction | TSP, ATSP | `start`, `rep`, `opt`, `verbose` |
| `"arbitrary_insertion"` | Arbitrary insertion | construction | TSP, ATSP | `start`, `rep`, `opt`, `verbose` |
| `"two_opt"` | 2-opt exchange | improvement | TSP, ATSP | `tour`, `two_opt_repetitions`, `rep`, `opt`, `verbose` |
| `"or_opt"` | Or-opt segment insertion | improvement | TSP, ATSP | `tour`, `max_segment`, `rep`, `opt`, `verbose` |
| `"three_opt"` | 3-opt exchange | improvement | TSP, ATSP | `tour`, `rep`, `opt`, `verbose` |
| `"sa"` | Simulated annealing | improvement | TSP, ATSP | `tour`, `local_move`, `temp`, `tmax`, `maxit`, `trace`, `rep`, `opt`, `verbose` |
| `"concorde"` | Concorde (exact, branch-and-cut) | external solver | TSP, ETSP | `clo`, `precision`, `keep_files`, `verbose`, `seed` |
| `"linkern"` | Chained Lin-Kernighan | external solver | TSP, ETSP | `clo`, `precision`, `keep_files`, `verbose`, `seed` |


Most heuristics accept the following common control parameters:

- `rep`: the number of random restarts. The best tour found is returned.
- `opt`: refine the constructed tour by local search: `"two"` (2-opt), `"or"` (Or-opt),
  `"three"` (3-opt), or `"two+or"` (2-opt and Or-opt alternately).
  The older `two_opt = TRUE` is deprecated; use `opt = "two"`.
- `start`: the first city for nearest neighbor and insertion algorithms.
- `verbose`: show progress and the parameters that are used.

If no method is given, `solve_TSP()` uses arbitrary insertion followed by 2-opt
improvement. Construction heuristics build a tour from scratch, while
improvement heuristics start with an existing tour (given as `tour`) and try to
shorten it. If no tour is supplied to an improvement heuristic, a random tour is
used.

## Tour construction heuristics

These algorithms create a tour from scratch.


### Nearest neighbor

The nearest neighbor algorithm [@Rosenkrantz1977] is a simple greedy procedure.
It starts with a randomly chosen city (or the city given by `start`) and
repeatedly appends the nearest city that has not been visited yet. It is very
fast, but typically has to make long "jumps" at the end of the tour to reach
the remaining cities.

The repetitive variant (`"repetitive_nn"`) runs the algorithm once from every
city and returns the shortest tour found.

### Insertion algorithms

All insertion algorithms [@Rosenkrantz1977] start with a tour consisting of a
single city and repeatedly insert a city $k$ that is not yet on the tour
between two consecutive tour cities $i$ and $j$ so that the increase in tour
length

$$d(i,k) + d(k,j) - d(i,j)$$

is minimal. They differ in how the city to be inserted is chosen:

- **Nearest insertion** chooses the city closest to any city on the tour.
- **Farthest insertion** chooses the city farthest from the tour. This first
  establishes an outline of the whole tour and fills in details later. In
  practice, farthest insertion often produces better tours than the other
  insertion variants.
- **Cheapest insertion** chooses the city with the lowest insertion cost.
- **Arbitrary insertion** chooses a random city. It is the fastest variant.

For distances that obey the triangle inequality, nearest and cheapest
insertion are related to Prim's minimum spanning tree algorithm [@Prim1957] and
guarantee tours that are at most twice the optimal length.

## Tour improvement heuristics

These heuristics modify existing tours to improve them. If no starting tour is 
specified then typically a random tour is used as the starting point.

2-opt is very effective. Many methods have for convenience the control
parameter `opt` which automatically applies a refinement to the constructed
tour. It can be `"two"` (2-opt), `"or"` (Or-opt), `"three"` (3-opt), or
`"two+or"` (2-opt and Or-opt alternately until neither improves the tour). For
example, `solve_TSP(x, method = "nn", opt = "two+or")`. Without a method,
`solve_TSP()` uses arbitrary insertion with `opt = "two"`. The older control
parameter `two_opt = TRUE` is deprecated.

### 2-opt

Two-opt [@Croes1958] repeatedly removes two edges from the tour and reconnects
the two resulting paths in the only other possible way (which is equivalent to
reversing a part of the tour) whenever this shortens the tour. The procedure
stops at a *2-optimal* tour, i.e., a local optimum for this neighborhood.
`"two_opt_repetitions"` can be used to restart the algorithm from random tours.

### Or-opt

Or-opt [@Or1976] moves a segment of 1 to `max_segment` consecutive cities
(default 3) to a different position in the tour, whenever this shortens the
tour. For symmetric problems, the segment may also be inserted in reverse
order. Or-opt can relocate a misplaced city or a small group of cities in a
single step, which 2-opt cannot do, while 2-opt removes crossing edges, which
Or-opt cannot do. The two methods complement each other, which is why
`opt = "two+or"` alternates between them. Or-opt only needs a few moves to be
checked and is about as fast as 2-opt.

### 3-opt

Three-opt [@Bock1958; @Lin1965] removes three edges, which splits the tour into
three parts, and reconnects them in the best of all possible ways (including
reversing parts). Its neighborhood contains all 2-opt and Or-opt moves, so a
*3-optimal* tour is also 2-optimal and Or-optimal. The price is a run time of
$O(n^3)$ for each pass over all triples of edges, which makes 3-opt practical
only for small to medium problems (up to a few thousand cities). For
asymmetric problems, only the reconnection that does not reverse any part of
the tour is used.

### Simulated annealing

Simulated annealing [@Kirkpatrick1983] uses random local moves (reversal of a
random sub-tour) and accepts moves that make the tour longer with a probability
that decreases as the temperature is lowered. This allows the search to escape
local optima. The implementation uses `stats::optim()` with method `"SANN"`.
The method is usually much slower than 2-opt and needs tuning of the cooling
schedule (`temp`, `tmax`, `maxit`). By default, only 10,000 evaluations are
used to keep the run time short, so a larger `maxit` is needed for competitive
results.

### Improving an existing tour

Improvement heuristics can be applied to any tour, including a tour that was
created outside of **TSP**. For example, we can refine a nearest neighbor tour
with 2-opt, Or-opt, and 3-opt, and then use a long simulated annealing run for
further improvement.

```{r improve}
library(TSP)
data(USCA50)
set.seed(1234)

nn <- solve_TSP(USCA50, method = "nn", start = 1)
opt2 <- solve_TSP(USCA50, method = "two_opt", tour = nn)
optor <- solve_TSP(USCA50, method = "or_opt", tour = opt2)
opt3 <- solve_TSP(USCA50, method = "three_opt", tour = optor)
sa <- solve_TSP(USCA50, method = "sa", tour = opt3, maxit = 50000)

c(nn = tour_length(nn), two_opt = tour_length(opt2),
  or_opt = tour_length(optor), three_opt = tour_length(opt3),
  sa = tour_length(sa))
```

We see how improvement methods reduce the tour length. The same refinements
can be requested directly when a tour is constructed using `opt`. 
We set the same random number seed inside the loop to get the
same nearest-neighbor tour. We run each algorithm with 10 random restarts.

```{r opt}

opts <- c("none", "two", "or", "two+or", "three")
## nearest neighbor breaks ties randomly. We reset the seed so every
## refinement starts from the same nearest neighbor tour.
len <- sapply(opts, function(o) {
  set.seed(1234)
  tour <- solve_TSP(USCA50, method = "nn", rep = 10,
    opt = if (o == "none") NULL else o)
  tour_length(tour)
})
len

## the optimal tour length (found by Concorde) is 14497
barplot(len / 14497 * 100 - 100, xlab = "opt",
  ylab = "percent excess over optimum in %")
```

## State-of-the-art solvers

Concorde [@Applegate2006] is currently one of the best exact solvers for
symmetric TSPs. It uses the branch-and-cut method [@Padberg1990] which
iteratively tightens a linear programming relaxation of the problem. The
Chained Lin-Kernighan heuristic [@Applegate2003], an extension of the
Lin-Kernighan heuristic [@Lin1973], is a very fast heuristic that finds
excellent tours for large instances. Both are accessed via the
`"concorde"` and `"linkern"` methods, but require that the Concorde executables
are installed separately. See `vignette("concorde")` for details.

## Asymmetric and Euclidean problems

All heuristics above work with asymmetric problems (`ATSP`). Solvers
that only handle symmetric problems use an automatic reformulation as a
symmetric TSP with twice as many cities (see `?reformulate_ATSP_as_TSP`).

Euclidean problems (`ETSP`) are converted into distance matrices for the
built-in heuristics, which needs memory proportional to the square of the
number of cities. Only `"concorde"` and `"linkern"` work with `ETSP` objects
directly.

## Reproducibility

Many methods are randomized (e.g., `"random"`, `"nn"` with a random start,
`"arbitrary_insertion"`, `"sa"`, and all methods with `rep > 1`). They use R's
global random-number stream. Calling `set.seed()` before `solve_TSP()` makes a
run reproducible, and every call advances the stream as any other R function
that draws random numbers does.

## Parallel execution

Repetitions (including `"repetitive_nn"`) are run using the **foreach**
package and can be executed in parallel by registering a backend before calling
`solve_TSP()`.

```{r parallel}
library(doParallel)
registerDoParallel()
solve_TSP(USCA50, rep = 100)
```

For parallel repetitions, one random number per repetition is drawn from R's global
stream in the main R process and used to seed the iteration (on the main
process or a worker). The results are therefore reproducible with `set.seed()`
independent of the backend and the number of workers.
